newsitem.title: USA: FTC cracks down on display rack fraud.
newsitem.headline: FTC cracks down on display rack fraud.

text.p: The government Tuesday announced it is cracking down on companies that fraudulently sell franchises that can cost investors tens of thousands of dollars to start up but often leave them penniless.

The Federal Trade Commission said it is starting an enforcement and education campaign to stop companies that sell licenses for in-store display racks, falsely claiming that entrepreneurs can earn hundreds of thousands of dollars selling trendy name-brand merchandise.
Consumers have lost more than $50 million in display rack scams since the beginning of 1995, the FTC said.

"The villains in these dramatic scenes are the opportunists who exploit a recognised corporate name to sell an unworkable business," Jodie Bernstein, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection said in a statement.
So far, six lawsuits have been filed in connection with the "Project Trade Name Games" programme, co-sponsored by eight states and several companies.
Entrepreneurs are often lured to display rack scams by newspaper advertisements that claim participants can earn "$100,000 or more" without quitting their full-time jobs.

Consumers buy the display racks and a license from the companies, which promise investors that they will receive timely merchandise, such as toys, stuffed animals and T-shirts from companies including Walt Disney Co., Warner Bros. and Coca-Cola Co., at wholesale costs.

Investors are also told that they will be able to place their racks in high-traffic locations, such as gas stations, gift shops, hotels and aiports, and simply need to restock and collect their earnings in their spare time.

Instead, investors often end up paying a large hidden set-up cost, are sold products that are extremely outdated at retail prices and are shocked to find their display racks hidden away in stores with little traffic.

One woman, who bought display stand franchises to have more time to spend with her eight-year-old daughter, earned an average 78 cents a day in the busy holiday shopping season rather than the $20 to $40 she was told she could count on making every day.

"While hundreds of consumers nationwide were losing their life's savings by investing in a toy distributorship company we targeted, my consumer protection division found company officers driving around Kansas City in luxury cars, wearing furs and dripping in diamonds," Kansas Attorney General Carla Stovall said.
Stovall led a case filed in her state against Parade of Toys, Inc., of Lenexa, Kan. and its successor corporation, Wonderful World of Toys, Inc., in Olathe, Kan.

Other lawsuits have been filed against Unitel Systems, Inc. of Plano, Texas; Carousel of Toys USA, Inc. of Lake Park, Fla.; Global Toy Distributors, Inc. of Staten Island, N.Y.; Toys Unlimited International, Inc. of West Palm Beach, Fla.; and another case that is sealed.

The FTC advises potential investors to contact the legal departments of the merchandise companies, ask for written confirmation of payments and earnings claims, check out locator companies and bring a lawyer or accountant on board to make sure the business is legitimate.
